title: Marrese v. American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons — Seventh Circuit discovery and preclusion stage
lead: Two surgeons denied professional-association membership sought rejection files in a federal antitrust suit after state litigation failed. The Academy’s contempt appeal and a separately certified preclusion appeal produced divided rulings on sensitive discovery, disobedience, and the continuing federal claim.

actors.name: R. Anthony Marrese and Michael Treister
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
actors.role: Association resisting discovery and invoking preclusion

actors.name: Judge Posner
actors.role: Author of the principal en banc opinion

actors.name: Judges Bauer, Eschbach, Flaum, Wood, and Cudahy
actors.role: Authors of separate writings with differing alignments

proceedings: After discovery refusal, the district court imposed $10,000 criminal contempt. The en banc Seventh Circuit reversed that judgment and, through a separately certified appeal, directed dismissal of the antitrust complaint with prejudice. The Supreme Court later reversed on other grounds.
limits: This is the January 1984 circuit stage, not current approval of its contested preclusion reasoning. The sensitive files were not categorically immune, the 2015 proportionality rule did not govern, and preclusion reached the court independently of contempt.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Membership denials led first to state-law claims
sections.cue: Preserve the two doctors’ different timing.
paragraphs: In 1976, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons rejected R. Anthony Marrese and Michael Treister without reasons or a hearing. They alleged professional benefits from membership, but it was unnecessary to practice or obtain hospital privileges. Both were certified and held privileges at several hospitals. They sued in Illinois on common-law and state constitutional theories requiring reasonable admission standards and a hearing, without a state antitrust claim.

The Illinois Appellate Court ordered Treister’s complaint dismissed because membership was not an economic necessity; the state supreme court denied review. Marrese’s case was stayed pending that appeal and later dismissed. His own dismissal followed filing of the federal suit, a timing point emphasized differently in the later separate opinions even though Posner described federal litigation as following defeat in state court.

sections.title: Federal antitrust allegations produced sensitive discovery and contempt
sections.cue: Trace how two appeals reached the en banc court.
paragraphs: The federal complaint sought damages and an injunction under Sherman Act section 1, alleging substantial Academy control over orthopaedic services and exclusion because the doctors competed too vigorously. The district court denied claim-preclusion dismissal and initially refused interlocutory certification. Those antitrust allegations remained unproved.

The doctors requested rejected-application files from 1970 through 1980. The Academy refused even after a confidentiality-protected production order, and the district court imposed criminal contempt and a $10,000 fine. The Academy appealed in No. 81-2671. Two panel decisions reversing contempt were successively vacated during rehearing.

Before the second en banc hearing, a newly assigned district judge certified the denial of dismissal under 28 U.S.C. section 1292(b). The court accepted No. 83-2683 and consolidated it with contempt. The pending collateral contempt appeal had not stripped the district court of authority over the underlying suit; criminal contempt itself was a final appealable judgment.

sections.title: Posner permitted review of the discovery order through contempt
sections.cue: Explain the route and the risk of disobedience.
paragraphs: The principal opinion distinguished orders directly appealable or otherwise reviewable before disobedience from ordinary discovery orders. Here contempt supplied a route to review, with sanctions remaining if the order proved valid. The Academy had not been punished for disrupting court, destroying records, or the manner of refusal; it refused to obtain review of an allegedly invalid production command.

Posner treated the order as falling with the precluded action but did not use contempt to reach the entire lawsuit’s merits. Preclusion came through the separately authorized interlocutory appeal. This was no general immunity for defying judicial orders.

sections.title: Tailored access could protect both association and proof
paragraphs: Independently of preclusion, the court found an abuse of discovery discretion. Production authority under Rule 37 operated alongside then-existing Rule 26 protection and sequencing powers. The judge needed to weigh hardship and available accommodations; postponement was easier to justify than permanent denial.

The Academy’s First Amendment claim did not create categorical immunity, but candid membership evaluations and professional exchanges implicated association. Exposing evaluators to depositions could deter participation, while withholding everything could prevent antitrust proof. The response required tailoring.

Possible methods included private judicial inspection of the doctors’ own files first, removal of names and identifying details verified against originals, counsel-only initial review, and later identification where particular leads justified it. These were alternatives, not mandatory steps for every case.

The actual order let the doctors see their files, lawyers discuss other files’ general contents with them, and identified individuals be deposed. The court found it insufficiently protective. Nonsensitive discovery might proceed first if other essential elements could defeat the claim; that sequence made no sense if the files alone sufficed. Sensitive material’s potential as settlement leverage reinforced management concerns. The 1983 Rule 26 amendment supported those responsibilities but postdated the challenged order.

sections.title: The principal preclusion rationale sought to bar a second litigation opportunity
sections.cue: Keep that reasoning distinct from the divided result.
paragraphs: Posner reasoned that the doctors could have asserted Illinois antitrust claims initially and that state and federal standards were materially equivalent on these allegations. Accepting exclusive federal Sherman Act jurisdiction while questioning its rationale, he viewed differences in treble damages as practically immaterial. His reading of section 1738 permitted greater preclusion than the rendering state might give without first resolving Illinois law.

That reasoning did not command a single unanimous theory. Cudahy characterized it as a plurality, and Flaum supported dismissal through a different rule calling for substantially contemporaneous litigation of related state and exclusively federal theories. The complaint-dismissal result therefore must be separated from assent to Posner’s explanation.

sections.title: Separate opinions split both contempt and preclusion
paragraphs: Bauer concurred in result, finding preclusion sufficient and saying he would approve the discovery reasoning if needed. Eschbach agreed discovery was an abuse of discretion and supported reversal of contempt, but opposed barring the federal claims. Flaum supported preclusion on his contemporaneous-litigation approach yet joined Wood on survival of criminal contempt, recognizing qualifications and equitable administration of his proposed rule.

Wood, joined by Cummings and Cudahy, regarded the district court’s confidentiality compromise as discretionary, noted the Academy’s opposition to proposed redaction, and rejected treating pursuit of evidentiary leads as abuse. He would sustain contempt despite reversal of the underlying order because the court had jurisdiction and preclusion was a defense. He also found waiver of a jury objection to the $10,000 fine after the Academy sought contempt review and failed to object to the announced amount. He favored affirming contempt while reconsidering private inspection and redaction before enforcing discovery.

Cudahy, joined by Cummings and Wood, separately opposed preclusion and joined Wood on discovery. Section 1738 required the rendering state’s rules, not an invented stronger federal bar. State courts could not hear Sherman Act claims, and unpleaded state and federal theories were not interchangeable. He disputed speculation about motives or desired damages and emphasized access for an exclusively federal claim, distinguishing factual estoppel, settlements, and statutory remedies.

sections.title: The two mandates ended both proceedings at this circuit stage
sections.cue: State the historical result and later limit.
paragraphs: The nine-member en banc court reversed criminal contempt and directed dismissal of that proceeding in No. 81-2671. In No. 83-2683 it reversed denial of the Academy’s motion and directed dismissal of the complaint with prejudice. Different coalitions supported the two results. The decision issued January 3, 1984, and was corrected January 10.

The Supreme Court later reversed at 470 U.S. 373 (1985) on other grounds. This stage’s disputed preclusion approach therefore should not be treated as current controlling law. The later classroom comparison with 2015 proportionality likewise was not part of the rule applied in 1984.
